stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many immunologists have assumed that the strength of a vaccine's initial antibody response determines how long its protection lasts. Immunologist Rana Okafor, however, has found that durable protection depends instead on memory B cells that settle in the bone marrow, and that these cells form only when a vaccine's antigen remains in the lymph nodes for at least two weeks. Her team has also shown that an experimental slow-release formulation keeps antigen in the lymph nodes for about three weeks. Taken together, these findings suggest that the slow-release formulation ______
choices: will provide lasting protection to every person who receives it
meets a requirement for forming the memory cells tied to lasting protection
keeps antigen in the lymph nodes longer than any other formulation does
works chiefly by strengthening the vaccine's initial antibody response
explanation: The term the two facts share is antigen staying in the lymph nodes. The memory cells form only when antigen stays at least two weeks, and the formulation keeps it there about three weeks. So the formulation meets that condition. The word 'only' makes this a necessary condition, not a guarantee, so the most you can conclude is that the formulation meets a requirement.

A.why: You treated 'form only when' as if it meant 'always form when.' Meeting a necessary condition does not guarantee the result, and nothing in the text supports 'every person.'

C.why: You used only the fact about the formulation and stretched it into a comparison with all other formulations. The text never compares it with anything else.

D.why: You went back to the popular view that the passage undercuts. Okafor ties durability to memory B cells, not to the initial antibody response.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In a four-year trial, agronomist Luis Ferreira planted winter rye between soybean seasons on half of a set of test plots. While the rye had no measurable effect on the following soybean yields, it substantially raised soil organic matter compared with the unplanted plots. Separate studies have established that soils richer in organic matter hold more water after rainfall. Taken together, these results suggest that planting winter rye between soybean seasons ______
choices: should help the soil retain more water after rainfall
should raise soybean yields by helping soil retain water
raises soil organic matter more than any other cover crop
should improve water retention in every soil and climate
explanation: The shared term is soil organic matter. Rye raises organic matter, and more organic matter means the soil holds more water. So rye should help the soil retain water. The yield result stayed the same, so the change you can infer is about water, not harvests.

B.why: You carried the chain into yields, but the passage says the rye had no measurable effect on soybean yields.

C.why: You took only the organic-matter fact and added a comparison with other cover crops. The trial tested only rye against unplanted plots.

D.why: You let 'every' slip past. One trial's plots cannot support a claim about all soils and climates.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Clinic case counts are a lagging measure of influenza's spread, because people typically seek care several days after they begin shedding the virus. Wastewater testing avoids this delay: infected people shed detectable viral material into sewage starting on roughly the first day of infection. This year, the city of Marlow began testing weekly samples from each of its sewage treatment plants. By adopting this approach, Marlow's health officials are likely able to ______
choices: prevent influenza from spreading among the city's residents
identify which individual residents have become infected
detect rising influenza infections before clinic counts show them
confirm influenza outbreaks only after clinics have reported them
explanation: The passage names the flaw in clinic counts, which is delay. It says wastewater picks up the virus from about the first day of infection, and that Marlow now tests wastewater. Linking these facts, Marlow can see rising infections earlier than clinic counts alone would show them.

A.why: You added an extra step. Detecting infections early might help officials respond, but the passage never says that detection stops the virus from spreading.

B.why: You assumed sewage samples can be traced to particular people. The passage describes pooled samples from treatment plants, not individual tests.

D.why: This reverses the point of the passage. Wastewater testing is described as a way to avoid waiting for clinic reports.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Seismologist Ines Varga studies slow slip events, episodes in which a fault moves gradually over weeks without producing strong shaking. Her models indicate that such events can shift stress onto neighboring locked sections of a fault, and earlier research has shown that added stress on a locked section increases the chance that it will rupture in a large earthquake. In 2023, GPS stations recorded a slow slip event beside a locked section of the offshore Kerran Fault. Varga's work therefore implies that the event ______
choices: will trigger a large earthquake on the locked section within weeks
released stress that had built up on the fault's locked section
made the Kerran Fault more hazardous than any other offshore fault
may have made a large earthquake on the locked section more likely
explanation: The shared term is stress on the locked section. Slow slip can add that stress, and added stress raises the chance of rupture. So the 2023 event may have raised the chance of a large earthquake. The words 'can' and 'chance' limit how strong the conclusion can be, which is why the answer says 'may have' and 'more likely.'

A.why: This is strength creep. The passage supports a higher chance of an earthquake, not a certain one within a set time.

B.why: You reversed the relationship. The passage says slow slip shifts stress onto locked sections, not that it relieves their stress.

C.why: You went past the chain with a comparison nobody made. The passage says nothing about other offshore faults.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: For centuries, printmakers etched their plates with nitric acid, which bites cleanly into metal but releases toxic nitrogen dioxide fumes that can damage the lungs of anyone working nearby. Ferric chloride, a salt solution, etches copper without giving off such fumes, although it works poorly on the zinc plates many printmakers favor. After years of using nitric acid on zinc, printmaker Hana Lindqvist switched to ferric chloride and began working only on copper plates. By making both changes, Lindqvist most likely ______
choices: avoided the harmful fumes while still being able to etch her plates
could keep etching the zinc plates she had used for years
made sharper prints than nitric acid would have allowed
eliminated every health risk involved in etching her plates
explanation: The passage gives two facts about ferric chloride: it releases no toxic fumes, and it works on copper but poorly on zinc. Lindqvist made two changes, switching to ferric chloride and to copper. Together they let her avoid the fumes and still etch her plates effectively.

B.why: You missed the qualification. Ferric chloride works poorly on zinc, which is why Lindqvist moved to copper.

C.why: You assumed the new method is better in quality. The passage compares the two methods only on fumes, not on how sharp the prints are.

D.why: You stretched 'avoids one hazard' into 'avoids every hazard.' The passage addresses only the nitrogen dioxide fumes.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Hydrologist Mara Quist compared streams in a semiarid basin before and after beavers were reintroduced. Although the beavers' dams did not change the total volume of water the streams carried over a year, they raised the nearby water table by as much as a meter. Earlier research had shown that in such basins, a higher water table releases groundwater into streams through the dry late-summer months. Quist's findings therefore suggest that beaver dams in the basin can ______
choices: increase the total amount of water the streams carry each year
raise the water table by a meter wherever beavers are introduced
help the streams keep flowing through the dry late-summer months
reduce how much groundwater the streams receive in late summer
explanation: The shared term is the water table. The dams raise it, and a higher water table feeds groundwater into streams in late summer. So the dams can help the streams keep flowing in the dry months. Annual volume did not change, so the effect you can infer is about timing, not total amount.

A.why: You picked the result that did not change. The passage says the dams did not change the total annual volume.

B.why: You used only the water-table fact and applied it to every place beavers live. The study covered one basin, and 'as much as a meter' is a maximum, not a typical figure.

D.why: You reversed the chain. A higher water table releases more groundwater into streams, not less.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because of its unusually adventurous harmonies, Friedrich Aldermann's String Quartet in E-flat has long been assumed to date from the final years of his life, around 1805. Musicologist Beatriz Llorente, however, points out that the only surviving manuscript of the quartet, written in Aldermann's own hand, is on paper from the Hollern mill. Aldermann's letters and dated scores show that he used Hollern paper only from 1776 to 1780, while he lived in Vienna. Llorente's evidence therefore suggests that the quartet ______
choices: was the final piece Aldermann completed before he left Vienna
was likely written during Aldermann's Vienna years, not late in life
was composed around 1805 on paper Aldermann had saved from Vienna
shows that adventurous harmony was typical of all Viennese composers
explanation: Link the facts through the Hollern paper. The manuscript in Aldermann's hand is on Hollern paper, and he used that paper only from 1776 to 1780 in Vienna. So he probably wrote the quartet during those years. The 'however' tells you the blank finishes Llorente's corrected view, not the old assumption.

A.why: You added more precision than the evidence gives. The paper puts the quartet somewhere in 1776–1780, not at the end of his time in Vienna.

C.why: You held on to the popular view that the passage undercuts. Aldermann's records show he used Hollern paper only until 1780, so this answer needs an assumption the passage contradicts.

D.why: You went past the chain to a claim about all Viennese composers. The evidence is about when one quartet was written, not about a whole group's style.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Chemical analysis of a fourteenth-century wool fragment dyed in the town of Serro revealed alizarin, a red dye compound that in medieval Europe came only from the roots of the madder plant. The analysis also found aluminum residue left by alum, a mineral salt used to bind dye to fibers. Tax records show that throughout the fourteenth century, all alum reaching Serro was imported from mines in Anatolia. The dyers who colored the fragment therefore ______
choices: grew their madder in fields near the Anatolian alum mines
used madder because alum could not be obtained in Serro
produced a redder wool than any other medieval European dyers
combined madder with alum that had come from Anatolian mines
explanation: You need three facts together. Alizarin means the dyers used madder. The aluminum residue means they used alum. All alum in Serro came from Anatolia. So they combined madder with Anatolian alum. Each part of the answer comes directly from a stated fact.

A.why: You added an extra step. The passage says where the alum came from, not where the madder was grown.

B.why: The fragment contains alum residue, and the tax records show that alum reached Serro, so alum was available there.

C.why: You went past the chain to a comparison with all other European dyers. The analysis describes only one fragment.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Folklorists have long assumed that Scandinavian ballads about a drowned bride began among fishing communities on the coast. Folklorist Ingrid Solheim's survey of 300 recorded versions complicates that view: every version that ends with the bride returning as a seabird was collected inland, along the Glomma river. Solheim also notes that all of the versions in the Haugen collection, one of her survey's sources, end with that seabird return. Taken together, these findings indicate that the Haugen versions ______
choices: were collected inland rather than in coastal fishing villages.
are older than the versions recorded in coastal fishing villages.
prove that the ballad first arose along the Glomma river.
include some endings in which the bride does not return.
explanation: Link the two facts through the term they share, the seabird ending. Fact 1: every surveyed version with the seabird ending was collected inland. Fact 2: every Haugen version has the seabird ending, and the Haugen versions are part of the survey. Take out the shared term and you get this: the Haugen versions were collected inland. Choice A says exactly that and adds nothing else.

B.why: The passage says nothing about when any version was composed or collected. You went past the chain and added a claim about age that neither fact supports.

C.why: This is the trap for this subtype: a broader claim that goes past the chain. Knowing where some versions were collected doesn't tell you where the ballad began. Solheim's survey only 'complicates' the coastal-origin view. It doesn't settle where the ballad came from, and 'prove' is much stronger than the evidence allows.

D.why: The passage says all of the Haugen versions end with the bride returning as a seabird, so none of them can end without her return. You reversed the second fact.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many coaches assume that extra sleep only makes athletes feel more rested and does nothing measurable to their bodies. Work by sports physiologist Imani Okafor challenges that view. She found that when competitive swimmers extended their sleep to ten hours a night, the amount of glycogen stored in their muscles rose. Other studies have shown that higher muscle glycogen delays fatigue during sustained high-intensity efforts. Taken together, these findings suggest that by extending their sleep, swimmers may also be ______
choices: delaying fatigue during sustained high-intensity efforts.
outperforming athletes in other sports who sleep less.
storing more glycogen because they already tire less.
feeling more rested without any change in their muscles.
explanation: The shared term is muscle glycogen. Okafor's study links extra sleep to more glycogen, and other studies link more glycogen to delayed fatigue. Remove the middle term and you get extra sleep → delayed fatigue. Choice A states that link and adds nothing else, and the passage's 'may' fits it.

B.why: You went past the chain. The passage only discusses swimmers and never compares them with athletes in other sports, so this comparison is a claim nobody established.

C.why: You reversed the chain. The passage says more glycogen leads to less fatigue. It never says less fatigue causes glycogen to build up, and in the passage the glycogen rise comes from sleep.

D.why: You picked the popular view the passage sets out to undercut. Okafor found a measurable change, higher muscle glycogen, so 'without any change in their muscles' contradicts her finding.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Scholars have long assumed that the anonymous motets in the Brenner Codex were copied in Paris, where most fourteenth-century motets originated. Musicologist Tomás Lindqvist disputes this. He observes that the codex marks syncopated rhythms with a small hooked stroke. He also notes that among all surviving fourteenth-century sources, only manuscripts produced at the cathedral of Ivrea use that stroke. If Lindqvist's observations are accurate, it follows that the Brenner Codex was ______
choices: composed by musicians who had trained at Ivrea.
produced at Ivrea rather than copied in Paris.
the first manuscript ever to use a hooked stroke.
copied in Paris by a scribe who had visited Ivrea.
explanation: The shared term is the hooked stroke. The Brenner Codex uses it, and only manuscripts produced at Ivrea use it. Since the codex is itself a surviving fourteenth-century source, it must be one of the Ivrea manuscripts. Choice B states that conclusion and nothing more.

A.why: You added an extra step. The evidence concerns where the manuscript was produced, not who composed the music or where they trained. Music can be composed in one place and copied in another.

C.why: You went beyond the chain. The passage says only Ivrea manuscripts use the stroke. It says nothing about which manuscript used it first, so 'first ever' is unsupported.

D.why: You held on to the older assumption. If only manuscripts produced at Ivrea use the stroke, a codex copied in Paris could not use it, whatever the scribe's travels.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Researchers gave two groups of older adults identical diets, except that one group also ate a daily serving of fermented cabbage. After twelve weeks, the groups' total fiber intake did not differ, but the cabbage group had markedly higher levels of the gut bacterium Lactobacillus plantarum. Earlier work had established that L. plantarum produces butyrate, a compound that strengthens the intestinal lining. These findings imply that eating fermented cabbage ______

benefits the gut mainly by raising a person's fiber intake.
strengthens the gut more than any other fermented food.
raises L. plantarum levels by first increasing butyrate.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Paleobotanists studying a 300-million-year-old coal seam found that fossil leaves of the seed fern Alethopteris have unusually thick cuticles, the waxy outer layer of a leaf. In living plants, thick cuticles are strongly associated with limiting water loss in dry or salty settings. Some researchers had assumed the seam formed in a uniformly wet swamp. However, Alethopteris leaves appear only in the seam's upper layers. Taken together, these findings support each of the following conclusions EXCEPT that ______
choices: the seam's upper layers preserve leaves with a trait linked to limiting water loss.
the assumption that the swamp stayed uniformly wet throughout may need revision.
the seam's lower layers formed under wetter conditions than any other seam of that age.
Alethopteris may have been suited to drier or saltier conditions than a wet swamp.
explanation: Each layer of evidence is about this one seam: a trait (thick cuticle) goes with resisting water loss, and that trait appears only in the upper layers. Linking those facts supports A, B, and D. Nothing in the text compares this seam with any other seam of the same age, so C adds a comparison nobody established. That's the claim the evidence does not support.

A.why: You rejected this because it only restates one fact and doesn't link the two. A plain restatement is still supported. The question asks which claim is NOT supported, not which one goes furthest.

B.why: You read the 'uniformly wet' assumption as the passage's own view. The word 'However' signals that the leaf evidence undercuts it, and 'may need revision' is hedged enough for the evidence to support.

D.why: You thought this went too far because no single sentence says it. But 'thick cuticles go with dry or salty conditions' and 'Alethopteris has thick cuticles' together give you exactly this, and 'may' keeps it modest. Linking two facts this way is the inference, not an extra step.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Health departments have traditionally tracked influenza through hospital admission records. Those records have two weaknesses: they include only patients sick enough to be admitted, and they typically reach officials weeks after infections occur. Wastewater testing avoids both problems. Nearly all infected people, including those with mild illness, shed viral fragments into sewage, and a sample can be analyzed within days. A city that adds wastewater testing to its surveillance could therefore reasonably expect each of the following EXCEPT to ______
choices: detect infections among residents whose illness never required hospital admission.
determine exactly how many residents are infected with influenza on a given day.
notice rising influenza activity sooner than admission records alone would allow.
receive results from a collected sewage sample within a matter of days.
explanation: The text says that viral fragments show up in wastewater, including from mild cases, and that results come back quickly. Connecting those facts to the weaknesses of hospital records supports A, C, and D. But knowing that fragments are present, even from nearly everyone infected, doesn't tell you an exact count of infected people. 'Exactly' goes past what the passage establishes, so B is the expectation the text does not support.

A.why: You thought this went beyond the text because it is never stated outright. Link 'records include only admitted patients' with 'mild cases shed fragments too' and this follows directly.

C.why: You saw a comparison and assumed it was unsupported. The passage gives both halves of the comparison: records arrive weeks late and samples are analyzed within days. Putting them together is the chain, not an added assumption.

D.why: You rejected this because it simply repeats a detail instead of linking facts. A repeated detail is still something the city can reasonably expect. The question asks for the claim the text fails to support.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Seismologists have long treated very small earthquakes as too weak to matter for forecasting large ones. However, a team monitoring a fault in northern Chile found that clusters of tiny quakes there consistently accompanied slow slip, a gradual movement of the fault that unfolds over weeks. Earlier research had shown that slow slip on this fault adds stress to the locked segment where the region's large earthquakes begin. Taken together, these findings support all of the following EXCEPT that ______
choices: slow slip on this fault is a gradual process that can continue for weeks.
the view that tiny quakes are useless for forecasting may not hold for this fault.
clusters of tiny quakes on the fault coincide with periods of added stress on the locked segment.
every cluster of tiny quakes on the fault will be followed by a large earthquake.
explanation: The shared term is slow slip. Tiny-quake clusters go with slow slip, and slow slip adds stress to the locked segment, so the clusters go with periods of added stress (C). That in turn undercuts the old view (B), and A restates a given fact. But added stress is not the same as a guaranteed rupture, and nothing says 'every' cluster leads to a large quake. D turns 'adds stress' into 'will be followed by,' which the evidence does not support.

A.why: You rejected this because it uses only one fact from the passage. A choice can repeat half the evidence and still be supported. Here you needed the one claim that fails, not the one that does the least.

B.why: You read the opening view as the passage's conclusion. 'However' sets up the new findings as an undercut, and the hedge 'may not hold' keeps this claim within what those findings show.

C.why: You thought this added a step because no single sentence links tiny quakes to stress. That link comes from cutting out the shared term, slow slip. That's exactly what 'taken together' asks you to do.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many coaches assume that a pre-race warm-up helps mainly by loosening the muscles. Physiologist Rhea Tamsin argues that temperature matters more. In her trials, runners who warmed up for fifteen minutes started their races with muscle temperatures about 1.5°C higher than runners who skipped the warm-up. Separate laboratory studies have found that each degree of warming increases how quickly muscle fibers can contract. Taken together, these findings suggest that, compared with runners who skip a warm-up, runners who warm up ______

begin their races with muscle fibers that can contract more quickly.
gain more contraction speed from each degree of muscle warming.
finish their races faster by a fixed amount for every degree.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Grammatical complexity was once thought to change at random as languages age. Linguist Oren Valdés disputes this. In his cross-language sample, languages acquired by large numbers of adult learners tended to shed their case endings, the suffixes that mark a noun's role in a sentence. Valdés also notes that a trading-port dialect of one language has been learned by far more adults than a highland dialect of the same language has. If Valdés is correct, the port dialect, compared with the highland dialect, has likely ______
choices: been learned by a greater number of adult speakers.
lost all of the case endings that it once had.
lost case endings at random rather than through learners.
retained fewer of its case endings over time.
explanation: The shared term is learning by many adults. Languages learned by many adults tend to shed case endings, and the port dialect has had far more adult learners than the highland dialect. So the port dialect has likely kept fewer case endings. The words 'tended' and 'likely' allow a difference in degree and nothing stronger.

A.why: You repeated one of the facts instead of linking the two. The passage already states that the port dialect had more adult learners. The blank asks what follows from that about its case endings.

B.why: This is strength creep. Valdés found that such languages 'tended to shed' case endings, which supports fewer endings. It does not support losing all of them.

C.why: You picked the older view that Valdés disputes. His evidence ties the loss of case endings to adult learners, not to chance.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Oysters build their shells from calcium carbonate, and the work takes more energy as seawater becomes more acidic. Ecologist Priya Nandakumar monitored two sites in a coastal bay. She found that water temperature was nearly identical inside and outside a seagrass meadow but that acidity was not. Because the grass draws carbon dioxide from the water during photosynthesis, water inside the meadow was consistently less acidic. Taken together, these findings imply that, compared with oysters just outside the meadow, oysters within it ______
choices: likely spend less energy forming their shells.
likely build their shells faster in warmer water.
save energy on shells whenever the pH happens to rise.
spend half as much energy forming their shells.
explanation: Link the facts through acidity. Less acidic water means oysters need less energy to build their shells, and the water inside the meadow is less acidic. So the oysters inside the meadow likely spend less energy forming their shells. This is the one difference between the two groups that both facts together support.

B.why: You missed the split in the findings. Temperature was the thing that stayed nearly the same at both sites, so warmer water can't explain any difference.

C.why: You used only the first fact. Any oyster needs less energy when acidity falls. This choice doesn't say how oysters inside the meadow compare with oysters outside it.

D.why: You read in a number the passage never gives. The text supports 'less energy' but not any particular amount, such as half.
